title: This Deep-Sea Hunter Is a Colony

segments.text: One hunter, or a colony? Trace that pale line through the water. Where would you say one animal ends and the next begins?
Look at this photograph from a dive off Puerto Rico. Start at the tip. Follow the row of clear bells down to the bend.
See how the pattern changes there? If these were just links in a chain, you'd expect the next link to do the same thing.
Here's the surprise. A siphonophore grows as a colony. The repeating parts are animals called zooids, and they stay attached.
Watch a swimming bell squeeze. Water shoots out of the opening. The push moves the bell and carries its neighbors along with it.
Farther down the stem, a tentacle trails in the water. Its stinging cells can catch prey. A feeding zooid has the mouth that takes the meal in.
So where does one hunter end? You can pick out the individual swimmers and feeders. But follow a meal or a single stroke, and you're watching the whole colony at work.
